scope: Grammar only; vocab numbers/counters are excluded

grammarPoint.title: ㅂ irregular: 춥다 → 추워요
grammarPoint.hint: Some descriptive and action verbs ending in ㅂ change that final consonant when a vowel-starting ending follows.
grammarPoint.description: Some descriptive and action verbs ending in ㅂ change that final consonant when a vowel-starting ending follows. This is a common pronunciation and spelling pattern, not a new tense.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: For a ㅂ-irregular stem, remove 다, drop final ㅂ and add 우 before -어: 춥다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For a ㅂ-irregular stem, remove 다, drop final ㅂ and add 우 before -어: 춥다 → 추워요. In 돕다 and 곱다, the resulting vowel can be 오 (도와요).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 오늘 날씨가 추워요. — The weather is cold today. The final ㅂ in 춥다 changes before the polite vowel ending, giving 추워요 rather than 춥어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Not every ㅂ-final verb is irregular: 입다 → 입어요 and 잡다 → 잡아요 remain regular. Learn exceptions with the vocabulary entry.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: ㄷ irregular: 듣다 → 들어요
grammarPoint.hint: Certain verbs whose stems end in ㄷ change it to ㄹ when followed by a vowel-starting ending.
grammarPoint.description: Certain verbs whose stems end in ㄷ change it to ㄹ when followed by a vowel-starting ending. The action stays the same; the stem spelling changes.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Remove 다 from selected ㄷ verbs and change ㄷ to ㄹ before vowel endings: 듣다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from selected ㄷ verbs and change ㄷ to ㄹ before vowel endings: 듣다 → 들어요, 걷다 → 걸어요. With consonant endings, ㄷ remains (듣습니다).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 음악을 들어요. — I listen to music. The stem 듣- becomes 들- before 어요, so the polite present form is 들어요 rather than 듣어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Not every ㄷ-final verb changes. 받다 → 받아요 and 닫다 → 닫아요 are regular; only certain verbs such as 듣다 and 걷다 change.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 르 irregular: 모르다 → 몰라요
grammarPoint.hint: Many stems ending in 르 change before 아요 or 어요, adding ㄹ to the preceding syllable.
grammarPoint.description: Many stems ending in 르 change before 아요 or 어요, adding ㄹ to the preceding syllable. This is why 'don't know' takes the form 몰라요.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Remove 다. For a 르-irregular stem, remove ㅡ from 르 and add ㄹ as the preceding syllable's final consonant; then choose 라/러: 모르다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다. For a 르-irregular stem, remove ㅡ from 르 and add ㄹ as the preceding syllable's final consonant; then choose 라/러: 모르다 → 몰라요; 부르다 → 불러요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 그 사람을 몰라요. — I don't know that person. 모르다 produces 몰라요 because the preceding syllable gains ㄹ and 르 becomes 라 before the polite ending.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not treat every 르 verb as identical. 따르다 → 따라요 does not use the doubling rule; the rule is lexical and needs examples.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 으 deletion: 쓰다 → 써요
grammarPoint.hint: A verb or descriptive verb whose stem ends in ㅡ often loses that vowel when an 아/어 ending is attached.
grammarPoint.description: A verb or descriptive verb whose stem ends in ㅡ often loses that vowel when an 아/어 ending is attached. The preceding vowel helps determine the new form.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Remove 다; remove stem-final ㅡ before 아요/어요, then check the preceding vowel: 쓰다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다; remove stem-final ㅡ before 아요/어요, then check the preceding vowel: 쓰다 → 써요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요, 예쁘다 → 예뻐요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 편지를 써요. — I write a letter. 쓰다 has only a stem-final ㅡ to drop, so it combines with 어요 as 써요, not 쓰어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is different from the 르 irregular doubling pattern. 쓰다 → 써요 has no extra ㄹ; 모르다 → 몰라요 does.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 해체: -아/-어 (casual speech)
grammarPoint.hint: In relaxed conversations with close friends or younger people, Korean often uses the same everyday ending without 요.
grammarPoint.description: In relaxed conversations with close friends or younger people, Korean often uses the same everyday ending without 요. Choosing this form depends on the relationship, not simply the sentence's meaning.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Make the same present form as -아요/-어요, then remove the polite 요: 가요

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Make the same present form as -아요/-어요, then remove the polite 요: 가요 → 가, 먹어요 → 먹어, 공부해요 → 공부해.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구야, 지금 가. — Hey, friend, I'm leaving now. 친구한테 '지금 가'라고 말해요: 가 is the casual form of 가요 used with someone close to the speaker.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use casual speech automatically with strangers, teachers or customers. The meaning stays similar but the social effect can be inappropriate.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 에게 / 한테 (to someone)
grammarPoint.hint: These particles mark the person or animal receiving a message, gift or action.
grammarPoint.description: These particles mark the person or animal receiving a message, gift or action. 한테 is common in speech, while 에게 appears frequently in writing.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Add 에게 or 한테 after the recipient: 친구에게/친구한테. The thing given normally takes 을/를: 친구한테 책을 줘요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 에게 or 한테 after the recipient: 친구에게/친구한테. The thing given normally takes 을/를: 친구한테 책을 줘요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구한테 편지를 써요. — I write a letter to a friend. 친구한테 편지를 써요 marks the friend as the recipient of the letter-writing action.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Place 에 marks locations or destinations, but 한테/에게 usually identify animate recipients. For a respected recipient, learn 께.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I write a letter to a friend.
I give a present to my younger sibling.

cards.englishHint: I send a photo to a friend.
I give water to a child.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 에게서 / 한테서 (from someone)
grammarPoint.hint: When an object or message comes from a person, these particles mark that person as the source.
grammarPoint.description: When an object or message comes from a person, these particles mark that person as the source. They are useful with receiving, hearing and learning.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Attach 에게서 or 한테서 to the source person: 친구에게서, 친구한테서. The received thing still takes 을/를: 친구한테서 책을 받았어요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 에게서 or 한테서 to the source person: 친구에게서, 친구한테서. The received thing still takes 을/를: 친구한테서 책을 받았어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님에게서 편지를 받았어요. — I received a letter from the teacher. 선생님에게서 편지를 받았어요 identifies the teacher as the person the letter came from.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use 에게서 for the recipient you GIVE something to; use 에게 or 한테. These are common but not interchangeable roles.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I received a letter from the teacher.
I got a photo from a friend.

cards.englishHint: I heard news from my younger sibling.
I borrowed a book from a friend.
I got a gift from Mom.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: -지 못하다 (long-form inability)
grammarPoint.hint: Use -지 못하다 to say someone cannot perform an action because of limited ability or circumstances.
grammarPoint.description: Use -지 못하다 to say someone cannot perform an action because of limited ability or circumstances. It is a longer alternative to 못 + verb.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Remove 다 from the action verb, attach 지 못하다, then conjugate 못하다: 가다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from the action verb, attach 지 못하다, then conjugate 못하다: 가다 → 가지 못해요; 먹다 → 먹지 못했어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 오늘은 학교에 가지 못해요. — I can't go to school today. 오늘은 학교에 가지 못해요 says the speaker is unable to go to school, with 가지 못해요 as the inability construction.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is inability, not simply choosing not to act. Compare 가지 않아요 ('don't go') with 가지 못해요 ('can't go').

lessonExamples.englishHint: I can't go to school today.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: ㅅ irregular: 짓다 → 지어요
grammarPoint.hint: Some verbs whose stem ends in ㅅ drop that final consonant before vowel-starting endings.
grammarPoint.description: Some verbs whose stem ends in ㅅ drop that final consonant before vowel-starting endings. The result can look shorter than the dictionary form.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: For selected ㅅ-irregular stems, remove 다 and the final ㅅ before the vowel ending: 짓다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For selected ㅅ-irregular stems, remove 다 and the final ㅅ before the vowel ending: 짓다 → 지어요, 낫다 → 나아요. The consonant remains before endings starting with consonants.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 새 집을 지어요. — We build a new house. 짓다 becomes 지어요 because its ㅅ is dropped before -어요, rather than producing 짓어요.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Not every ㅅ-final verb is irregular: 웃다 → 웃어요 and 씻다 → 씻어요. Those verbs retain their ㅅ.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: ㅎ irregular: 파랗다 → 파래요
grammarPoint.hint: Some colour and descriptive words ending in ㅎ drop that consonant or change their vowel when they conjugate.
grammarPoint.description: Some colour and descriptive words ending in ㅎ drop that consonant or change their vowel when they conjugate. The form is important for natural descriptions.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Selected ㅎ-irregular stems change before vowel endings: 파랗다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Selected ㅎ-irregular stems change before vowel endings: 파랗다 → 파래요, 그렇다 → 그래요, 어떻다 → 어때요. Before a noun, 파랗다 → 파란 하늘.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 하늘이 파래요. — The sky is blue. 하늘이 파래요 uses 파래요 because 파랗다 is an irregular descriptive stem.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 좋다 is a regular ㅎ-final word: 좋아요, 좋은. Do not treat all words written with final ㅎ as irregular.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: ㄹ deletion before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ
grammarPoint.hint: Stems ending in ㄹ often lose ㄹ when an ending beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ is added.
grammarPoint.description: Stems ending in ㄹ often lose ㄹ when an ending beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ is added. This is common in formal speech and honorifics.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: When an ending beginning ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ follows, remove the stem-final ㄹ: 살다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: When an ending beginning ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ follows, remove the stem-final ㄹ: 살다 → 삽니다, 만들다 → 만드세요, 알다 → 아는 사람.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 서울에 삽니다. — I live in Seoul. 서울에 삽니다 shows that 살다 loses ㄹ before formal -ㅂ니다, so 삽니다 is correct.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not drop ㄹ before every ending: 살아요 keeps it, and 살면 keeps it. Check the initial consonant of the attached ending.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 와/과 (and / with nouns)
grammarPoint.hint: 와/과 joins nouns or marks someone you do an action together with.
grammarPoint.description: 와/과 joins nouns or marks someone you do an action together with. It is slightly more common in writing or careful speech than 하고.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: After a noun ending in a vowel add 와, after a consonant add 과: 사과와 바나나, 책과 연필. For doing something together: 친구와 영화 봐요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After a noun ending in a vowel add 와, after a consonant add 과: 사과와 바나나, 책과 연필. For doing something together: 친구와 영화 봐요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 사과와 바나나를 샀어요. — I bought apples and bananas. 사과와 바나나를 샀어요 uses 와 to join two object nouns into one list.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: The choice 와 versus 과 depends on the preceding syllable, not the next word. Compare the more conversational 하고 and (이)랑.

cards.englishHint: I go together with a friend.
I bought a bag and shoes.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: (이)랑 (and / with)
grammarPoint.hint: (이)랑 is a conversational way to say 'and' or 'with' between nouns or people.
grammarPoint.description: (이)랑 is a conversational way to say 'and' or 'with' between nouns or people. It commonly appears in everyday informal speech.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Use 이랑 after a final consonant and 랑 after a vowel: 책이랑 공책, 친구랑 영화. The two forms play the same connecting role.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 이랑 after a final consonant and 랑 after a vowel: 책이랑 공책, 친구랑 영화. The two forms play the same connecting role.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구랑 영화를 봐요. — I watch a movie with my friend. 친구랑 영화를 봐요 means the speaker watches a movie together with a friend.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For a formal report or academic writing, 와/과 is usually a better choice. Don't attach the consonant form 이랑 after a vowel-ending noun.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I watch a movie with my friend.
I bought a book and a notebook.

cards.englishHint: I play with my younger sibling.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 께서 (honorific subject)
grammarPoint.hint: 께서 is a respectful subject marker used for people the speaker honors.
grammarPoint.description: 께서 is a respectful subject marker used for people the speaker honors. It can replace 이/가 when describing a teacher, elder or another respected person.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Put 께서 after the respected person's noun or title: 선생님께서, 할머니께서. Use an honorific verb form when appropriate: 선생님께서 오세요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 께서 after the respected person's noun or title: 선생님께서, 할머니께서. Use an honorific verb form when appropriate: 선생님께서 오세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님께서 오세요. — The teacher is coming (respectfully). 선생님께서 들어오세요 uses 께서 to honor the subject and -시- in 들어오세요 to honor the action's performer.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 께서 is a SUBJECT marker. It is not the same as 께, which marks a respected recipient, or ordinary 이/가.

cards.englishHint: The teacher is reading a book.

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks

grammarPoint.title: 께 (to a respected person)
grammarPoint.hint: 께 is a respectful alternative to 에게/한테 when someone important to the speaker receives a gift, message or action.
grammarPoint.description: 께 is a respectful alternative to 에게/한테 when someone important to the speaker receives a gift, message or action.
grammarPoint.structurePattern: Put 께 after the recipient's name or title: 선생님께, 할머니께. Keep the object separately marked: 선생님께 편지를 드려요.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 께 after the recipient's name or title: 선생님께, 할머니께. Keep the object separately marked: 선생님께 편지를 드려요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 선생님께 편지를 드려요. — I give the teacher a letter (respectfully). 선생님께 편지를 드려요 marks the teacher as the respected recipient of the letter.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 께 marks the person receiving something; 께서 instead marks the respected subject doing the action. Do not confuse the two.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I give the teacher a letter (respectfully).

cards.englishHint: I ask the professor a question (respectfully).

sourceReferences: Darakwon, Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning (publisher contents); NIKL teacher portal for meaning checks
